commands.name: review
commands.description: review changes - uncommitted by default, or a [commit|branch|pr]
commands.template:
Review a set of code changes and give feedback the author can act on.

What to review: $ARGUMENTS

## Working out what to review

1. Nothing given: every change not yet committed.
   - `git diff` for what is not staged, `git diff --cached` for what is;
   - `git status --short` for files that are new and untracked.
2. A commit hash, full or short: that commit - `git show <hash>`.
3. A branch name: this branch against it - `git diff <branch>...HEAD`.
4. A pull request, as a link or a number: `gh pr view <it>` for its context and `gh pr diff <it>` for the change, when the GitHub CLI is available.

Use judgement where the input could be read more than one way.

## Reading around the change

A diff on its own is not enough. Once you know which files changed, read each of them whole: code that looks wrong in isolation can be right in context, and the other way round.
- Read untracked files in full.
- Follow the control flow and error handling around each change.
- Look for the project's own conventions: AGENTS.md, CONVENTIONS.md, .editorconfig, linters' settings.

## What to look for

**Bugs** - the main thing.
- Wrong logic, off-by-one errors, conditions the wrong way round.
- Missing guards, wrong branches, code that can never run.
- Edge cases: empty, missing or null input, error paths, races.
- Security: injection, bypassed authorisation, data exposed.
- Error handling that swallows failures, throws where nothing catches it, or returns errors callers do not check.

**Fit** - does the change belong in this codebase?
- Does it follow the patterns around it, and use the abstractions that already exist?
- Could deep nesting be flattened with early returns or a helper?

**Performance** - only where it is plainly a problem: quadratic work on unbounded input, a query per item, blocking I/O on a hot path.

**Changed behaviour** - point out anything that now behaves differently, especially if it may not have been intended.

## Before calling something a problem

Be sure. Review only what changed, not code that was already there. Do not report a bug you are unsure of - look further first - and do not invent unlikely failures; if an edge case matters, describe the real situation in which it breaks. If you still cannot tell, say that you are not sure rather than stating it as a fault.

Do not police style. Check that a convention is really broken before saying so, accept the simplest option when it is reasonable, and raise style only where it clearly goes against this project's own rules. Deep nesting is worth raising regardless.

## Tools

Read the surrounding code, search the project for how similar problems are handled, and check the documentation of a library before calling its use wrong.

## The report

1. For each bug, say plainly why it is one.
2. Give each finding an honest severity; do not inflate it.
3. Say under which inputs, environments or conditions the problem appears, so its severity can be judged at a glance.
4. Keep the tone factual and helpful - neither accusing nor flattering.
5. Write so the point is clear on a quick read.
6. Leave out anything that does not help: no praise, no thanks.

commands.name: data-analytics
commands.description: Analyse data to answer a question with evidence - data quality checks, metric breakdowns, KPI reports, trend and cohort analysis, charts, dashboards, and a written finding with a recommendation. Use when the user hands over a CSV, spreadsheet or database export and asks what it shows, why a number moved, or for a report built from it.
commands.template:
# Data analysis

**Which Python.** When the `MCODE_PYTHON` environment variable is set, use that
interpreter wherever this skill says `python`: `"$MCODE_PYTHON" scripts/...` in
bash, `& $env:MCODE_PYTHON scripts/...` in PowerShell. MCode ships it with
python-docx, python-pptx, openpyxl, pandas, pypdf, pypdfium2, reportlab, lxml and
Pillow installed, so the install checks below can be skipped. It has no pip
console scripts; run tools as modules (`-m`).

Work from the question to the evidence, and show every number's source.

## 1. Pin down the question

Restate what is being asked in one sentence, which metric answers it, over which
period and population. If a definition is genuinely ambiguous ("active user",
"revenue" gross or net), ask with the question tool before computing anything.

## 2. Look at the data before trusting it

```
python scripts/profile_table.py "data.csv"
```

Run it from this skill's folder with the bash tool. Note blanks, columns that are
mostly but not entirely numeric, mixed date formats, duplicates and ragged rows.
For .xlsx inputs, use the xlsx skill's dump script first, or read the sheet with
pandas. Write down each cleaning decision you make; it goes into the report.

## 3. Compute in a script

- Write the analysis as a Python script in the project (pandas when available;
  ask before installing it) and run it with bash. Keep the script: it is the
  audit trail and lets the numbers be regenerated.
- Check totals against the raw data (row counts, sums) after every join or filter.
- Compare like with like: same period length, same population, and say when a
  difference is too small or the sample too thin to mean much.

## 4. Chart what matters

- One chart per finding. Bar charts for comparisons, lines for time, scatter for
  relationships; no pies beyond three slices, no 3D.
- Title each chart with the finding, label axes with units, start value axes at
  zero for bars.
- Save charts as PNG or SVG files with matplotlib; small diagrams can go straight
  into the reply as a ```mermaid or ```svg block (see the visualizer skill).

## 5. Write it up

Lead with the answer, then the two or three findings that support it, each with
its number and chart, then caveats (data gaps, assumptions, cleaning), then what
to do next. If a deliverable file was asked for, produce it (Markdown, HTML, or a
workbook via the xlsx skill) and call `present_files` with it.

For multi-step work, track the steps with the task tool.

commands.name: deep-research
commands.description: Investigate a question thoroughly across many sources and write a report with citations. Use when the user asks for in-depth research, a comparison of options, a literature or market scan, fact-checking a claim from several angles, or a written briefing - not for a quick lookup one fetch can answer.
commands.template:
# Deep research

## 1. Frame it

Write the question, what a useful answer looks like (a recommendation, a
comparison table, a timeline), the scope (dates, regions, sources to prefer or
avoid) and the depth wanted. If any of these would change the work and is not
clear, ask with the question tool first.

Break the question into three to six sub-questions and record them with the task
tool, one task each.

## 2. Gather

- MCode fetches pages with `webfetch` but has no search engine of its own. Start
  from sources the user named, official documentation, standards bodies, primary
  data (statistics offices, company filings, papers), and pages those sources
  link to. When you need a starting point you do not have, ask the user for
  links or search terms rather than inventing URLs.
- For wide questions, hand sub-questions to subagents with the actor tool
  (`spawn`, `subagent_type: "explore"`), each with its sub-question, the sources
  to start from, and what to report back: findings with the URL and a short
  quote for each. Bind each to its task with `task_id`. Keep working while they
  run; their results arrive as notifications.
- For every claim you intend to use, keep the URL, the date of the source and
  the exact supporting sentence.

## 3. Weigh

- Prefer primary sources over summaries of them, recent over old where things
  change, and independent sources that agree over a single loud one.
- When sources disagree, say so and explain which you trust more and why.
- Separate what the evidence shows from your own inference, and mark the latter.

## 4. Write the report

Save it as a Markdown file in the project (or the format asked for):

1. The answer, in a few sentences.
2. Findings, one section per sub-question, each claim followed by its citation
   `[n]`.
3. Disagreements and open questions.
4. Sources: a numbered list with title, publisher, date and URL.

Call `present_files` with the report. In the reply, give the answer and the two
or three findings that matter most; do not paste the whole report.

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Create, read, edit and check Microsoft Word documents (.docx, .dotx). Use whenever a Word file is the input or the deliverable - reports, letters, contracts, proposals, filled templates - or when the user wants text, headings or tables pulled out of one, a document restructured, or a Word file converted to PDF.
commands.template:
# Word documents

**Which Python.** When the `MCODE_PYTHON` environment variable is set, use that
interpreter wherever this skill says `python`: `"$MCODE_PYTHON" scripts/...` in
bash, `& $env:MCODE_PYTHON scripts/...` in PowerShell. MCode ships it with
python-docx, python-pptx, openpyxl, pandas, pypdf, pypdfium2, reportlab, lxml and
Pillow installed, so the install checks below can be skipped. It has no pip
console scripts; run tools as modules (`-m`).

A .docx file is a zip of XML parts. Read it with the script below, write it with
python-docx, and always check the result before handing it over.

## Reading a document

Run the extractor from this skill's folder with the bash tool:

```
python scripts/docx_text.py "path/to/file.docx"
```

It prints headings as `#` lines, list items as `- ` lines, tables as `| a | b |`
rows and the style of other styled paragraphs in brackets. Add `--max-chars 20000`
for long documents. Use it before editing so you know the structure and styles.

## Writing or editing a document

1. Check that python-docx is available: `python -c "import docx"`. If it is not,
   ask before installing it (`python -m pip install python-docx`).
2. Write a short script into the project (for example `build_report.py`) and run
   it with bash. Keep the script, so the document can be rebuilt after changes.
3. When editing an existing file, open it with `docx.Document(path)` and change
   paragraphs and runs in place; save to a new name unless the user asked to
   overwrite. A template keeps its look only if you reuse its styles
   (`paragraph.style = "Heading 1"`) instead of setting fonts by hand.
4. Use real structure: heading styles for headings, `add_table` with a table
   style for tables, list styles for lists, page breaks rather than blank lines.

## Checking the result

- `python scripts/check_ooxml.py "out.docx"` confirms the package is sound.
- Run `docx_text.py` on the output and read it back against the request.
- To see the pages, convert with LibreOffice when it is installed
  (`soffice --headless --convert-to pdf out.docx`) and look at the PDF.

## Handing it over

Call `present_files` with the finished document (and the PDF, if you made one)
so the user can open it in the side panel. Say in one line what the document
contains; do not paste its text into the reply.

## Pitfalls

- Text split across runs: a phrase may be spread over several `w:r` elements, so
  search the paragraph's full text, then rewrite its runs.
- Do not build a .docx by writing XML strings unless python-docx cannot express
  the change; if you must, change a copy and run the checker.
- `.doc` (the old binary format) cannot be read this way; convert it with
  LibreOffice first.

commands.name: html-to-video
commands.description: Render an animated HTML page into an MP4 video with a headless browser and ffmpeg, frame by frame so timing is exact. Use when the user builds or debugs anything that turns HTML, CSS or JavaScript animation (CSS keyframes, GSAP, canvas) into a video file - product demos, animated explainers, social clips, or several scenes joined into one.
commands.template:
# HTML to video

Screen-recording a page in real time drops frames and drifts. Instead, drive the
animation clock yourself, capture one frame at a time, and encode the frames.

## Check the tools

- Node.js and Playwright: `npx playwright --version`; the browser is installed
  with `npx playwright install chromium`.
- ffmpeg: `ffmpeg -version`.

Ask before installing anything; show the commands.

## 1. Make the page controllable

The page must render any moment on request. Expose one function:

```
window.renderAt = (seconds) => { /* put every animation at this time */ }
```

- CSS animations: set `animation-play-state: paused` on everything and
  `animation-delay: -<seconds>s`, or use `document.getAnimations()` and set each
  animation's `currentTime`.
- GSAP: build a paused timeline and call `timeline.seek(seconds)`.
- Canvas or requestAnimationFrame loops: draw from a time argument instead of
  from `performance.now()`.

Fix the page size (for example 1920x1080), load fonts locally, and wait for
`document.fonts.ready` before the first frame.

## 2. Capture frames

Write a script in the project (for example `render.mjs`) that opens the page in
Playwright at the video size, and for frame `n` from 0 to `duration * fps` calls
`renderAt(n / fps)`, waits for two animation frames, and saves
`frames/frame_%05d.png`. Run it with `node render.mjs` through bash; when `node` is not
installed, MCode's bundled Node.js is `$MCODE_NODE` (`"$MCODE_NODE" render.mjs`).

## 3. Encode

```
ffmpeg -y -framerate 30 -i frames/frame_%05d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 out.mp4
```

`-pix_fmt yuv420p` keeps the file playable everywhere. For several scenes, render
each to its own MP4 with the same size and fps, list them in a text file
(`file 'scene1.mp4'`) and join with `ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy all.mp4`.
Add audio with `-i music.mp3 -shortest`.

## 4. Verify

- `ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration:stream=width,height,r_frame_rate out.mp4`
  must match the intended duration, size and fps.
- Pull a few frames back out (`ffmpeg -ss 2.5 -i out.mp4 -frames:v 1 check.png`)
  and look at them with the read tool: fonts loaded, nothing clipped, animation
  at the expected state.
- Call `present_files` with the video.

commands.name: learn-everything
commands.description: Turn a document, paper, book chapter, web page or topic into a structured course and teach it step by step with explanations, exercises and quizzes. Use when the user wants to learn, study, review or master something, asks to be taught a PDF or article chapter by chapter, wants practice questions or a test, or comes back to continue a course.
commands.template:
# Teaching a course

## Start

1. Find the material: a file the user attached or named (read it; for PDFs use
   the pdf skill), a URL (fetch it with `webfetch`), or a topic with no source.
2. Ask with the question tool: current level, goal (exam, job, curiosity), time
   per session, and preferred language if it is unclear.
3. Look for an existing course file (`course/<topic>/progress.md`). If one exists,
   say where the learner left off and continue from there.

## Plan the course

Write `course/<topic>/plan.md` in the project: 4-10 units, each with its learning
goals as things the learner will be able to do, the source sections it draws on,
and prerequisites. Keep units short enough for one session. Show the plan and
adjust it to the learner's feedback.

## Each unit

1. Explain the idea plainly, building on what the learner knows; one worked
   example; a diagram when structure matters (see the visualizer skill).
2. Quote or cite the source section so the learner can read the original.
3. Check understanding with 2-4 questions of mixed kinds: recall, apply to a new
   case, spot the mistake. Use the question tool for multiple choice.
4. Grade answers with specific feedback: what was right, the misconception if
   any, and a hint before revealing the answer.
5. Record in `progress.md`: unit done, score, weak points to revisit.

## Keep it working

- Adapt: slow down and add examples after wrong answers; skip ahead when answers
  are consistently right.
- Start each later session with two quick review questions on earlier weak points.
- After the last unit, give a mixed final assessment and a short summary sheet
  (`course/<topic>/summary.md`), and call `present_files` with it.
- Never make up facts that are not in the source; when going beyond it, say so.

commands.name: less-ai-tone
commands.description: Clean the machine-written feel out of a finished piece of writing (去AI味, 去掉AI腔) by applying only the rules listed in this skill - stock openers and closers, reflexive contrasts, lists of three, dash and colon habits, inflated vocabulary, translationese, unsupported claims, recap paragraphs, chatbot framing. Text no rule matches is left exactly as it was, and the structure of the piece is never changed. Use after a draft is written, when the user asks to make it sound less like AI, more natural or more human, in Chinese or English.
commands.template:
# Less AI tone

This is a rewrite with a fixed list. Each rule below names a tell you can point
at in the text and says what to do with it. Change only what a rule catches.
Anything no rule catches stays word for word, and the piece keeps its
sections, their order, its argument and every fact in it. The goal is text
that no longer reads as generated, not text in your own voice: do not add
first-person asides, slang, jokes or choppy short paragraphs to make it seem
human.

## Before you start

1. Read the whole piece and name its genre: report, essay, speech, marketing
   copy, fiction, technical documentation, academic writing, a message. Several
   rules depend on it.
2. If the user gave a sample of their own writing or a style to follow, read
   it first. It decides what counts as the piece's normal punctuation,
   register and sentence length, and it wins over any rule here.
3. Work on a copy. Keep the original so the two can be compared at the end.

## The rules

Each rule: what to look for, and what to do. "Leave" lists what looks similar
but is not the tell.

### 1. Stock openers and closers

Look for: a first sentence that restates the question or announces the topic
("在当今快速发展的时代", "In today's fast-paced world",
"Let's dive in"), and a last paragraph that begins with a summing-up phrase
("总而言之", "综上所述", "In conclusion", "Overall") and says again what
was already said.

Do: start with the first sentence that carries information; end on the last
point that adds something. Delete the frame, not the content inside it - if
the closing paragraph holds a point made nowhere else, keep that sentence.

Leave: a summary the genre calls for (an abstract, an executive summary, the
conclusion section of a paper).

### 2. Signposting that announces instead of saying

Look for: "值得注意的是", "不难发现",
"It's worth noting that", "It is important to note", "Notably,".

Do: drop the phrase and state the point. If the point then feels unimportant,
it probably was; leave that judgment to the user and keep the sentence.

### 3. The reflexive contrast

Look for: "不是……而是……", "不仅仅是……更是……", "与其说……不如说……",
"It's not just X, it's Y", "This isn't about X - it's about Y", used where no
one had claimed X.

Do: state Y directly. Keep the contrast only where the text or its reader
actually holds the view being corrected. When the same pattern appears more
than twice in a piece, keep at most the strongest one.

### 4. Dashes, colons and quotation marks as a habit

Look for: a dash ("——", " - ", "—") used to set off an aside or a reveal in
sentence after sentence; a colon before a one-word or one-phrase payoff;
scare quotes around ordinary words.

Do: rewrite with ordinary sentence structure - a comma, a clause, or two
sentences. Keep dashes where the author's own writing uses them this way (see
"Before you start"); change only the excess.

### 5. Lists where prose was needed

Look for: groups of exactly three adjectives, nouns or clauses again and again
("高效、便捷、智能", "fast, reliable, and scalable"); bullet lists and bold
labels in what should be continuous prose; a heading over every two
paragraphs.

Do: keep the items that are specific, merge or drop the filler, and turn a
list back into sentences when the genre is prose. Keep lists that are real
lists (steps, requirements, an inventory) and the formatting the genre expects
(documentation, slides).

### 6. Inflated words

Look for, in Chinese: 赋能, 助力, 打造, 全方位, 至关重要, 不可或缺, 无缝, 画卷,
and words of the same kind. In English: delve,
tapestry, landscape (for a field), leverage, robust, seamless, pivotal,
crucial, vibrant, testament, realm, navigate (for anything but travel),
unlock, elevate, embark.

Do: use the plain word the sentence means, or drop the word if the sentence
stands without it. Keep a term that is the precise technical word in its field.

### 7. Translationese (Chinese)

Look for: "进行" before a verb ("进行分析" -> "分析"); "对……进行……";
unnecessary "被" passives; long chains of "的"; "一个" before every noun;
"通过……来……" where the means is obvious; sentences built on English
word order with the verb at the end of a long modifier.

Do: rewrite in natural Chinese word order with the same meaning. For literary
writing, judge against the piece's own style rather than against plain prose.

### 8. Claims without support

Look for: "研究表明", "众所周知", "Studies show",
"Experts agree", "Many people believe" with no study, data or expert named.

Do: if the text gives the source or figure elsewhere, attach it here. If it
gives none, soften to what the text can stand behind, or ask the user for
the source. Never invent a source, a number or a name.

### 9. Hedging and empty intensifiers

Look for: stacks of qualifiers ("在一定程度上可能会", "may potentially",
"somewhat arguably"); intensifiers that add nothing ("非常",
"truly", "incredibly", "extremely") on sentence after sentence.

Do: keep one qualifier where the uncertainty is real, drop the rest. Keep
intensifiers only where the emphasis is the point.

### 10. Chatbot framing

Look for: "希望以上内容对您有所帮助", "当然！", "好的，以下是",
"I hope this helps", "Feel free to ask", "Great question", any sentence
addressed to the person who asked for the text rather than to its reader.

Do: delete it. The text is for its readers, not a reply in a chat.

## What never changes

- Facts, figures, names, dates, quotations and citations.
- The order and division of sections, and what each paragraph argues.
- Technical terms, code, commands and anything inside quotation marks that is
  a quotation.
- Sentences no rule above matches, even if you would have written them
  differently.

## When you finish

1. Compare with the original. Every change must trace to a rule; undo any that
   does not.
2. Read the result once as its intended reader would. If a rewrite made a
   sentence less clear, put the original back.
3. Give the user the cleaned text, then a short list of what you changed,
   grouped by rule number, with a count for each. Say plainly if some rule
   matched nothing.

If the user wants a file changed rather than text in the reply, edit the file
and keep a copy of the original beside it unless they say not to.

commands.name: mcode-guide
commands.description: Answer questions about MCode itself and change its display settings - where instructions, skills and commands go, how subagents, tasks, permissions, models and MCP servers work, and how to switch theme, font sizes, diff style or language. Use when the user asks how to do something in MCode, why it behaves a certain way, or asks it to change one of its own settings.
commands.template:
# MCode, for its own users

Answer from what is below. If a question goes past it, say what you are unsure
of and point to the Settings page most likely to hold the answer instead of
guessing.

## Settings you can change directly

`get_desktop_settings` reads, and `set_desktop_setting` changes, these keys:
`theme`, `ui_font_size`, `code_font_size`, `diff_style` and `language`. Read
first to see the allowed values, change what was asked, and say what changed.
Everything else - models and providers, MCP servers, permissions, shortcuts,
voice, sounds - is changed by the user in Settings; tell them which page.

## Instructions

- A project's `AGENTS.md` (also `CLAUDE.md` and `.mcode/rules.md`) is read into
  every conversation in that project.
- The global AGENTS.md, kept in MCode's data folder and opened from Settings,
  applies to every project; the project's own file wins where they disagree.

## Skills

- Folders with a `SKILL.md`. MCode ships built-in ones (this is one); users add
  their own under `.mcode/skills/<name>/` in a project or `skills/<name>/` in
  MCode's data folder. A user skill replaces a built-in one of the same name.
- Typing `/name` in a message loads that skill into it (up to three per
  message). The slash menu lists every skill, and the composer's plus menu
  offers them as chips. The skill-creator skill explains how to write one.

## Commands

Markdown files under `.mcode/commands/` become slash commands; the text after
the command name fills `$ARGUMENTS`, `$1`, `$2`. MCP servers' prompts appear in
the same menu.

## Subagents and tasks

- The agent can hand work to subagents with the actor tool: `spawn` runs one in
  the background, `run` waits for it. They appear as pills in the conversation
  and in the 子智能体 (Subagents) tab of the side panel, with their own
  transcripts.
- The task tool keeps the conversation's task list (T1, T1.1 ...), shown in the
  information card's task list.

## Permissions

The access level in the composer decides what runs without asking: ask for
changes, approve-for-me (routine edits and commands run, risky ones are checked),
or full access. Settings can set any tool to always allow, ask or deny. A
refused call is not run; the refusal, and any reason given, goes straight back
to the agent, which carries on another way in the same turn. Only Stop ends a
turn.

## Modes

Plan mode (from the composer) reads and describes a plan without changing files.
`/compact` summarises a long conversation to free context.

## Side panel

Files the agent produces or presents open in the side panel: Word, Excel,
PowerPoint and PDF previews, HTML pages, images and video, diffs and review, a
terminal and a browser.

commands.name: memory-search
commands.description: Query MCode's own record of past conversations and memory files directly with read-only SQL, for what the memory and history tools cannot answer - counting, grouping, filtering by tool or outcome, following a whole run of tool calls, or checking a claim a memory note makes against what actually happened. Use after memory and history searches came up short or too coarse.
commands.template:
# Searching memory and history with SQL

## In short

The `memory` and `history` tools cover most look-ups. Reach for this skill when
the question is about *many* records at once - how often, which ones, in what
order - or when a note in memory needs checking against the raw record. Open
everything read-only and never write to it.

## Where the data is

Everything lives in MCode's data folder: the folder that holds `memory/`. The
memory paths in your system prompt start with it, so take the part before
`memory` as `<data>`.

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Search index (SQLite) | `<data>/index/search.db` |
| Memory files | `<data>/memory/<global \| projects/<id> \| sessions/<id>>/<name>.md` |
| A conversation's details | `<data>/storage/session/<session id>/info.json` |
| Its messages | `<data>/storage/session/<session id>/message/<message id>.json` |

The JSON files are the record; the index is built from them and from the
memory files, and can lag a few seconds behind a message that was just
written.

### Tables in `search.db`

- `history_part(part_id, session_id, message_id, project, kind, tool_name, body, search_body, time_created)`
  - one row per indexed piece of a message;
  - `kind` is `text`, `reasoning`, `file`, `tool`, `summary` (a compaction
    summary) or `error` (what a failed reply ended with);
  - `tool_name` is set for tool rows; a tool row's `body` is the tool name, its
    input as JSON, then its output or error;
  - `project` is the project id: the same for every folder of one repository,
    `global` for folders outside any repository;
  - `time_created` is milliseconds since 1970.
- `history_session(session_id, project, indexed_at)` - one row per indexed
  conversation.
- `memory_doc(path, scope, scope_id, type, body, search_body, fingerprint, indexed_at)` - one
  row per memory file; `type` is `memory`, `notes`, `progress`, `checkpoint` or
  `free`.
- `history_part_fts` and `memory_doc_fts` - full-text tables over `search_body`,
  joined on `rowid = id`.
- `search_body` is `body` with a space between each pair of neighbouring
  Chinese, Japanese or Korean characters, so a search for part of a word in
  those scripts matches; it is empty when the body has none of them, and the
  `_fts` tables read it through a view that falls back to `body`. Read `body`;
  search the `_fts` tables, and cut a query in those scripts the same way -
  `MATCH '"配 置"'` for 配置.

## How to open it

Use the Python that ships with MCode when `MCODE_PYTHON` is set (`"$MCODE_PYTHON"`
in bash, `& $env:MCODE_PYTHON` in PowerShell), otherwise `python`. Open the file
read-only with a URI, so nothing can change it even by mistake:

```python
import sqlite3, pathlib, sys
db = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
con = sqlite3.connect(f"{db.resolve().as_uri()}?mode=ro", uri=True)
con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
for row in con.execute(sys.argv[2]):
    print(dict(row))
```

Save it as a scratch script outside the project, pass the database path and the
query, and keep result sets small with `LIMIT`.

## Queries that come up

Tool calls in one conversation, in order:

```sql
SELECT message_id, tool_name, substr(body, 1, 300) AS preview
FROM history_part
WHERE session_id = '<session id>' AND kind = 'tool'
ORDER BY time_created;
```

Which tools this project used most over the last week:

```sql
SELECT tool_name, count(*) AS n
FROM history_part
WHERE project = '<project id>' AND kind = 'tool'
  AND time_created > (strftime('%s','now') - 7*86400) * 1000
GROUP BY tool_name ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 20;
```

The project id of a conversation is in `history_session`; the same id names
its folder under `memory/projects/`.

Every conversation that mentions a phrase, newest first:

```sql
SELECT p.session_id, max(p.time_created) AS last_seen, count(*) AS hits
FROM history_part_fts f JOIN history_part p ON p.id = f.rowid
WHERE history_part_fts MATCH '"deploy" "staging"'
GROUP BY p.session_id ORDER BY last_seen DESC LIMIT 20;
```

What the user said, word for word, about a rule:

```sql
SELECT p.session_id, p.time_created, substr(p.body, 1, 500) AS said
FROM history_part_fts f JOIN history_part p ON p.id = f.rowid
WHERE history_part_fts MATCH '"always"' AND p.part_id LIKE '%/text'
ORDER BY p.time_created DESC LIMIT 20;
```

Only a user message's words have a part id ending in `/text`
(`<session>/<message>/text`); the assistant's text rows end in their own part
ids, so that condition keeps what the user said.

## Checking a memory note

1. Find the note with the `memory` tool and read the file.
2. Pick its distinctive words and search `history_part_fts` for them.
3. Read the rows that match in full with the `history` tool (`get` with the
   `part_id`), or open the message JSON.
4. Keep the note when the record supports it; otherwise correct it, or mark it
   `[unverified]` if nothing confirms or contradicts it.

## Rules

- Read only. Never `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `VACUUM` or attach the file in
  write mode, and never edit the JSON store.
- Do not copy tokens, keys or other secrets you find in the record into your
  reply or into memory.
- Say which conversation and time a finding comes from, so the user can check
  it.

commands.name: merge
commands.description: Finish a branch once its work is done and its tests pass - offer to merge it locally, push it and open a pull request, keep it, or throw it away, then carry out the choice and tidy up the worktree it lived in. Use when implementation is complete and the user needs to decide how the work goes back into the main line.
commands.template:
# Finishing a branch

## In short

Check the tests, find out where you are, offer a fixed set of choices, do the
one picked, and clean up only what this work created. Say at the start that you
are using this skill to finish the branch.

Nothing destructive happens without an explicit yes from the user.

## Step 1: the tests pass

Run the project's test suite (`npm test`, `cargo test`, `pytest`, `go test ./...`
- whatever the project uses).

If anything fails, stop and report:

```
<N> tests fail, so the branch is not ready to merge or publish:

<the failures>
```

Do not offer the choices below until they pass.

## Step 2: where the branch lives

```bash
git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-dir
git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir
git branch --show-current
```

| What you find | Choices to offer | Clean-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same directories (ordinary checkout) | all four | none needed |
| Different directories, on a branch | all four | Step 5 |
| Different directories, detached HEAD | three: no local merge | none - someone else manages this folder |

## Step 3: the base branch

The system prompt names the repository's default branch; that is usually the
base. Confirm it with:

```bash
git merge-base HEAD <default branch>
```

If it is not clear which branch this one grew from, ask with the `question`
tool:
- header: `Base branch`
- question: `This branch seems to come from <base>. Is that right?`
- options: `Yes, <base>` - merge back into it; `Another branch` - the user names it

A subagent uses the branch it found.

## Step 4: offer the choices

With the `question` tool:
- header: `Finish`
- question: `The work is done and tested. What should happen to <branch>?`
- options:
  - `Merge here` - merge it into <base> in this repository
  - `Pull request` - push the branch and open a pull request
  - `Keep` - leave the branch as it is for now
  - `Discard` - delete the branch and its commits

On a detached HEAD, leave out `Merge here`, and say that the pull request would
be pushed as a new branch.

A subagent does not choose for the user: it keeps the branch and reports.

### Merge here

Work from the main checkout, never from inside the worktree being finished:

```bash
cd "$(git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir)/.."
git checkout <base>
git pull
git merge <branch>
```

Run the tests again on the merged result. Only when the merge and the tests both
succeed, clean up (Step 5) and then delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -d <branch>
```

If the merge stops on conflicts, the note in the command's result says what to
do; follow it rather than resolving the conflict yourself.

### Pull request

```bash
git push -u origin <branch>
```

Then open the pull request against <base> with the host's own tool if the user
has one set up (for example `gh pr create`), with a title and a body that list
what changed and how it was tested. Without such a tool, give the user the
branch name and the link the push printed.

Keep the worktree: review comments will need it.

### Keep

Report `Branch <branch> kept; its worktree stays at <path>.` and change nothing.

### Discard

Ask once more, with the `question` tool:
- header: `Discard`
- question: `This deletes <branch>, every commit on it and the worktree at <path>, and cannot be undone. Go ahead?`
- options: `Cancel` - keep everything; `Delete it` - discard for good

Only `Delete it` continues; `Cancel` goes back to Step 4. Then, from the main
checkout, clean up (Step 5) and remove the branch:

```bash
git branch -D <branch>
```

## Step 5: clean up the worktree

Only after `Merge here` or `Discard`.

```bash
git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-dir
git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
```

- Same directories: an ordinary checkout, nothing to remove.
- The worktree is under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`: this work created it, so
  remove it from the main checkout:

  ```bash
  git worktree remove "<worktree path>"
  git worktree prune
  ```

- Anywhere else: something other than this workflow made it. Leave it in place
  and tell the user where it is.

`git worktree remove` refuses when the worktree has uncommitted changes. Do not
add `--force`; tell the user what is left there.

## Quick reference

| Choice | Merges | Pushes | Keeps the worktree | Deletes the branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Merge here | yes | - | - | yes |
| Pull request | - | yes | yes | - |
| Keep | - | - | yes | - |
| Discard | - | - | - | yes, forced |

## Mistakes to avoid

- **Offering choices on failing tests.** A merge or pull request of broken work
  costs more than the wait.
- **Asking an open question.** "What next?" gets a vague answer; give the four
  choices (three when detached).
- **Removing the worktree for a pull request.** The review is not over yet.
- **Deleting the branch before removing its worktree.** git refuses, and a half
  clean-up is left behind.
- **Discarding without the second question.** Deleting commits is the one step
  that cannot be taken back.
- **Removing a worktree this work did not create.** Only folders under
  `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/` are yours to remove.

commands.name: modern-python-toolchain
commands.description: Set up and run Python projects with uv, ruff and pyright. Use when starting a new Python project, a task needs Python and the project has no pyproject.toml yet, dependencies need adding or locking, or the user asks for linting, formatting, type checking or a virtual environment.
commands.template:
# Python with uv, ruff and pyright

## Check what is there

- `uv --version`, `python --version` (on Windows `py -0` lists installed Pythons).
- In an existing project, read `pyproject.toml`, any `requirements*.txt`,
  `uv.lock`, `poetry.lock` or `setup.cfg` first, and keep the tool it already
  uses unless the user wants to move.

If uv is missing, ask before installing it. The official installers are
`powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"`
on Windows and `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh` elsewhere; show
the command and let the user choose.

## New project

```
uv init my-project            # or `uv init` inside an existing folder
cd my-project
uv add requests               # runtime dependency
uv add --dev ruff pyright pytest
uv run python main.py
```

uv creates `.venv` and `uv.lock`; commit the lock file, not the venv.

## Everyday commands

- Run anything in the project environment: `uv run <command>`.
- Add or remove: `uv add pkg`, `uv remove pkg`; upgrade one: `uv lock --upgrade-package pkg`.
- Recreate the environment from the lock: `uv sync`.
- Pin the Python version: `uv python pin 3.12`.

## Lint, format, type-check, test

```
uv run ruff check --fix .
uv run ruff format .
uv run pyright
uv run pytest
```

Configure them in `pyproject.toml`:

```
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B"]

[tool.pyright]
typeCheckingMode = "standard"
```

Run all four before saying Python work is done, and report what each said.

## Moving from requirements.txt

`uv add -r requirements.txt` imports the list into pyproject.toml; check the
versions it resolved, then remove the old file only if the user agrees.

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Read, create, combine, split, rotate and fill PDF files. Use whenever a PDF is the input or the deliverable - extracting text or tables, answering questions about a paper or a contract, merging or reordering pages, producing a report, invoice or certificate as PDF, filling a form - or when the user points at a passage in a PDF.
commands.template:
# PDF files

**Which Python.** When the `MCODE_PYTHON` environment variable is set, use that
interpreter wherever this skill says `python`: `"$MCODE_PYTHON" scripts/...` in
bash, `& $env:MCODE_PYTHON scripts/...` in PowerShell. MCode ships it with
python-docx, python-pptx, openpyxl, pandas, pypdf, pypdfium2, reportlab, lxml and
Pillow installed, so the install checks below can be skipped. It has no pip
console scripts; run tools as modules (`-m`).

## Reading

- The read tool can open a PDF directly when the model supports it; for long
  files, pull text page by page instead:
  `python scripts/pdf_tool.py text "file.pdf" --pages 1-5`
- `python scripts/pdf_tool.py info "file.pdf"` shows page count, size, metadata,
  encryption and form fields - run it first on an unfamiliar file.
- No text comes back from a scanned PDF. Say so, and offer OCR (for example
  `ocrmypdf`, if the user installs it) rather than guessing at the content.
- Tables: extracted text loses columns. When layout matters, try `pdfplumber`
  (ask before installing it) and check a few rows against the page.

Run the script from this skill's folder with the bash tool. It needs pypdf
(`python -m pip install pypdf`) and says so when it is missing - ask before
installing.

## Pointing at a passage

When your answer rests on a specific passage, call `pdf_locate` with the file, a
short fragment copied exactly as it appears in the PDF, and its page number. The
side panel opens the PDF at that place so the user can see the source.

## Changing pages

```
python scripts/pdf_tool.py merge out.pdf a.pdf b.pdf
python scripts/pdf_tool.py pages in.pdf excerpt.pdf --pages 2-5
python scripts/pdf_tool.py split in.pdf pages/
python scripts/pdf_tool.py rotate in.pdf turned.pdf --degrees 90 --pages 1,3
```

Inputs are never overwritten; write outputs under new names in the project.

## Creating a PDF

- From a document you write: build it as HTML (or Markdown turned into HTML) and
  print it with a headless browser, or write a Word file with the docx skill and
  convert it with LibreOffice (`soffice --headless --convert-to pdf`).
- From code: reportlab gives exact control over layout (ask before installing it).
- Put the generating script in the project so the PDF can be rebuilt.

## Forms

`info` lists the form fields. Fill them with pypdf's
`PdfWriter.update_page_form_field_values`, then open the result to check the
values show. A form with no fields needs text drawn onto the page instead.

## Checking and handing over

Re-run `info` and `text` on what you produced, and look at a page or two with
the read tool. Then call `present_files` with the PDF so it opens in the side
panel, and say in one line what it contains.

commands.name: powershell-reference
commands.description: Get PowerShell right before running or handing it over - syntax, quoting and escaping, pipelines, operators, parameters, cmdlets, calling native programs, error handling, encoding, and what differs between Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7. Use when writing, explaining, reviewing or fixing a PowerShell command or script. Not for Bash-only work, cmd.exe batch files, or Windows administration that is not about PowerShell itself.
commands.template:
# PowerShell reference

The fastest way to be wrong in PowerShell is to write Bash with PowerShell's
name on it. Settle which PowerShell you are writing for, check the forms below
that most often go wrong, and when unsure, ask the shell itself rather than
memory.

## Which PowerShell

- `powershell.exe` is **Windows PowerShell 5.1**, the one every Windows ships
  with. `pwsh.exe` is **PowerShell 7** (7.4 and later are current). When the
  user does not say, and the command runs through `powershell.exe` or the
  machine's default shell, write for 5.1 and say that you assumed it.
- Find out rather than guess: `$PSVersionTable.PSVersion` prints the version;
  `Get-Command pwsh -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` says whether 7 is installed.
- A script that must run on both keeps to what 5.1 accepts.

## What 5.1 does not have

| Written for 7 | In 5.1 instead |
|---|---|
| `a && b`, `a \|\| b` | `a; if ($?) { b }` and `a; if (-not $?) { b }` |
| `$x ? 'y' : 'n'` | `if ($x) { 'y' } else { 'n' }` |
| `$a ?? 'default'`, `$a ??= 1` | `if ($null -eq $a) { 'default' } else { $a }` |
| `$obj?.Name`, `$list?[0]` | test for `$null` first |
| `ForEach-Object -Parallel` | `Start-Job`, or a plain loop |
| `ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable` | work with the `PSCustomObject` it returns |
| `Get-Content -AsByteStream` | `Get-Content -Encoding Byte` |
| `Join-Path a b c` (several children) | nest `Join-Path` calls |

## Quoting and escaping

- Single quotes are literal: `'$HOME stays as written'`. Double quotes expand
  `$var`, `$($expression)` and escapes.
- The escape character is the backtick, not the backslash: `` "`n" `` is a
  newline, `` "`t" `` a tab, `` "`$" `` a literal dollar sign. A backslash is an
  ordinary character, so Windows paths need no doubling.
- A single quote inside single quotes is written twice: `'it''s'`.
- Here-strings: `@'` ... `'@` is literal and `@"` ... `"@` expands; the closing
  marker must start at column 0 on a line of its own.
- `$env:NAME` reads and sets environment variables; `$NAME` is a PowerShell
  variable, and `%NAME%` means nothing here.
- Characters such as `@`, `{`, `}`, `(`, `)`, `;`, `,` and a leading `-` are
  syntax. When a native program needs them passed through untouched, quote the
  argument, or put `--%` (stop-parsing) before the arguments.

## Calling programs

- A path with spaces is run with the call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\Tool\tool.exe" --flag`.
  Without `&` it is only a string.
- A script in the current folder needs `.\script.ps1`.
- A native program's exit code is `$LASTEXITCODE`; `$?` is only true or false.
  Check `$LASTEXITCODE` after anything whose failure matters.
- 5.1, and 7 before 7.3, can mangle arguments that contain double quotes or
  are empty when passing them to a native program. On 7.3 and later
  `$PSNativeCommandArgumentPassing` decides; in 5.1 prefer `--%`, or pass JSON
  and similar through a file or standard input.
- `2>&1` on a native program in 5.1 turns each stderr line into an error
  record and makes `$?` false even on success; read the exit code instead.

## Pipelines carry objects

- The pipeline passes .NET objects, not text: filter with `Where-Object`,
  shape with `Select-Object`, loop with `ForEach-Object`, measure with
  `Measure-Object`. Parse text only when it really is text.
- `Format-Table` and `Format-List` are for the screen; nothing after them in
  the pipeline can use the result.
- Common Bash habits and their PowerShell forms: `ls` -> `Get-ChildItem`,
  `cat` -> `Get-Content`, `grep` -> `Select-String`, `head -n 5` ->
  `Select-Object -First 5`, `tail -n 5` -> `Get-Content -Tail 5`, `wc -l` ->
  `(Get-Content f | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`, `which` ->
  `(Get-Command x).Source`, `touch` -> `New-Item -ItemType File`,
  `mkdir -p` -> `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force`, `rm -rf` ->
  `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force`, `export X=1` -> `$env:X = '1'`.
- Comparison operators are words: `-eq -ne -lt -gt -le -ge -like -match
  -contains -in`. `>` is a redirection, never "greater than". Comparisons
  ignore case unless written `-ceq`, `-cmatch` and so on.
- Put `$null` on the left: `$null -eq $x`. With an array on the left the
  comparison filters the array instead of answering yes or no.

## Errors

- Most cmdlet failures are non-terminating: the script carries on and
  `try`/`catch` never sees them. Add `-ErrorAction Stop` to the call, or set
  `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` at the top of a script, when failure
  should stop it.
- `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` hides the message but still records the
  error; test the result rather than assuming it worked.
- `Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process` and similar may ask for confirmation, which
  hangs a non-interactive run. Pass `-Confirm:$false` when the action is
  intended, and never add `-Force` to a command without knowing what it
  overrides.

## Files and encoding

- In 5.1, `Set-Content` and `Add-Content` write the system's ANSI code page,
  and `Out-File` and `>` write UTF-16. Pass `-Encoding UTF8` when another tool
  will read the file (5.1's UTF8 adds a byte order mark; 7's `utf8` does not,
  and `utf8BOM` does).
- PowerShell 7 defaults to UTF-8 without a byte order mark everywhere.
- `Get-Content` returns an array of lines; add `-Raw` for one string.
- `-LiteralPath` treats `[` and `]` in a file name as ordinary characters;
  `-Path` treats them as a wildcard.

## Scripts

- The execution policy can refuse to run a `.ps1`. Do not change the machine's
  policy on your own; for one run, `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File
  script.ps1` leaves the setting alone - and say that is what you did.
- `param()` must be the first statement of a script. Functions must be defined
  before the line that calls them.
- `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` near the top catches misspelt variables.

## Check against the shell, not memory

- `Get-Help <Cmdlet> -Parameter <Name>` and `Get-Command <Cmdlet> -Syntax`
  show what this machine's version really accepts. `Get-Help about_Quoting_Rules`,
  `about_Parsing`, `about_Operators` and `about_Redirection` hold the rules
  above in full (run `Update-Help` only with the user's agreement, since it
  downloads).
- To test a fragment's syntax without running it:
  `[System.Management.Automation.Language.Parser]::ParseInput($code, [ref]$null, [ref]$errors)`
  and look at `$errors`.
- When you explain a rule to the user, say which version it holds for.

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Create, read, edit and check PowerPoint presentations (.pptx). Use whenever a deck is the input or the deliverable - pitch decks, reviews, training slides, a presentation filled from a template - or the user wants a deck's text or notes pulled out, slides reordered or restyled, or a presentation converted to PDF or images.
commands.template:
# Presentations

**Which Python.** When the `MCODE_PYTHON` environment variable is set, use that
interpreter wherever this skill says `python`: `"$MCODE_PYTHON" scripts/...` in
bash, `& $env:MCODE_PYTHON scripts/...` in PowerShell. MCode ships it with
python-docx, python-pptx, openpyxl, pandas, pypdf, pypdfium2, reportlab, lxml and
Pillow installed, so the install checks below can be skipped. It has no pip
console scripts; run tools as modules (`-m`).

Plan the story first, then build slides with python-pptx, then look at what you
built. A deck is judged by its pages, so checking visually matters here.

## Reading a deck

```
python scripts/pptx_outline.py "deck.pptx"
```

Run it from this skill's folder with the bash tool. It lists every slide's title,
text, tables, layout name and speaker notes (`--no-notes` leaves notes out).

## Planning

Before writing code, write the outline in your reply or in a scratch file: one
line per slide saying the point it makes. Aim for one idea per slide, a title
that states the takeaway ("Costs fell 12% after the move", not "Costs"), and
roughly 10-15 slides unless told otherwise. When the design matters, settle it
first in design notes, as the slide-deck part of your instructions describes.

## Building

1. Check python-pptx (`python -c "import pptx"`); ask before installing it with
   `python -m pip install python-pptx`.
2. Write the build script into the project and run it with bash; keep it so the
   deck can be rebuilt.
3. With a template, open it (`Presentation("template.pptx")`) and add slides from
   its layouts (`prs.slide_layouts`), filling placeholders rather than drawing
   free text boxes, so the template's fonts and colours carry through.
4. Without a template, set 16:9 (`prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)`,
   `prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)`), pick two fonts and a small palette, and use
   them on every slide.
5. Keep text short: at most about six bullets of a line each. Put detail in the
   speaker notes (`slide.notes_slide.notes_text_frame.text`).
6. Charts: use python-pptx's native charts (`add_chart`) so they stay editable;
   images only for photos and diagrams.

## Checking

- `python scripts/check_ooxml.py "deck.pptx"` confirms the package is sound.
- Run the outline script on the result and compare it with your plan.
- If LibreOffice is installed, export a PDF
  (`soffice --headless --convert-to pdf deck.pptx`) and read pages with the read
  tool to catch text running off slides or overlapping shapes. Fix and rebuild.

## Handing it over

Call `present_files` with the deck (and the PDF if you made one). Give the user
the outline in a few lines, not the slide text.

commands.name: research-paper-writing
commands.description: Draft, revise and polish academic papers - abstract, introduction, related work, method, experiments, conclusion - and build them with LaTeX. Use when the user writes or edits a paper or thesis chapter, asks whether a passage reads well, wants notes or a draft in another language turned into publication-quality English, wants a reviewer-style critique before submission, or needs the LaTeX to compile.
commands.template:
# Research papers

## Before editing

Read the whole draft (or the section and its neighbours) first. Find the venue's
template and page limit, the paper's single main claim, and the evidence for it.
Ask for any of these that you cannot find.

## Section by section

- **Abstract**: problem, gap, what was done, the main result with a number, why
  it matters. No citations, no undefined abbreviations.
- **Introduction**: context, the specific problem, why existing work falls short,
  the contribution as a short list, a pointer to the results.
- **Related work**: group by idea, not by paper; end each group by saying how
  this work differs.
- **Method**: enough to reproduce; define every symbol at first use; one notation
  throughout.
- **Experiments**: setup (data, baselines, metrics, seeds), main results table,
  ablations tied to claims, limitations. Every claim in the text points at a
  table or figure.
- **Conclusion**: what was shown and what remains, without new claims.

## Editing prose

- Keep the author's meaning; flag rather than silently change a claim.
- One idea per paragraph, topic sentence first; cut hedges that add nothing.
- Prefer active voice and concrete verbs; keep tense consistent.
- When translating a draft, translate meaning, then edit for how a native writer
  in the field would put it.
- Show changes as a diff (edit the .tex file) or, for pasted text, the revised
  paragraph followed by a short list of what changed and why.

## Review pass

Read as a critical reviewer and list: unsupported claims, missing baselines,
unclear contributions, notation clashes, figures that cannot be read in grey,
and anything over the page limit. Rank by how much each would hurt acceptance.

## LaTeX

- Build with `latexmk -pdf main.tex` (or `-xelatex` for non-Latin scripts) through
  bash; if latexmk is missing, run `pdflatex`, `bibtex`, then `pdflatex` twice.
- Fix errors from the first one in the log; warnings about undefined references
  usually vanish after the second run.
- Check the PDF with the pdf skill: page count, figures placed, references
  resolved (no `??`). Call `present_files` with the PDF.

commands.name: reverse-engineer-anything
commands.description: Reverse engineer native, managed, Electron/JavaScript, packaged, firmware, and browser targets with REA. Use shipped-artifact or requested runtime evidence to explain features, compare versions, decompile code, or guide a reconstruction. Skip REA for ordinary source-repository architecture analysis.
commands.template:
# REA

Use REA when a claim depends on a shipped binary or package, decompilation,
passive application runtime evidence, or comparison with
behavior not established by available source. For ordinary analysis of a
complete source repository, use normal repository tools and do not run REA
readiness or provider commands.

## Connect only when needed

Installing this skill supplies instructions; it does not register the REA MCP
server, install analysis engines, or add tools to an already-running agent.

If REA tools are available and their registration is not known to be stale,
proceed directly to the target. Do not run diagnostics or setup before every
investigation. Use the connected server's actual tool list and input schemas;
a skill installed from repository main may describe capabilities absent from
an older npm release. Keep complete inline Evidence when that server does not
advertise retained references.

If tools are absent, a call is blocked by the client, or a required provider is
unavailable, read [connection and recovery](references/connection-and-recovery.md).
Diagnose the observed blocker, continue useful supported work, and resume the
original task after repair. Client approval, shell PATH, registration and engine
availability have different remedies; avoid repeating setup for all of them.

1. Diagnose without changing REA or client configuration. `npx` may download
   the package and write to npm's cache. For Codex, run
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0 doctor --client codex --json`. Substitute the current
   supported client: `claude_code`, `claude_desktop`, `codex`, `cursor`,
   `gemini_cli`, `windsurf`, `devin`, `opencode`, `antigravity`, `copilot_cli`,
   `commandcode`, `vscode`, `grok_build`, `omp`, or `grok_bot`. `grok_bot` has no local
   file registration: doctor reports the Grok Bot chat step, and setup does not
   write `mcp.json`. If the client is unknown, use `doctor --json` and
   inspect its registration results before choosing a setup scope.
2. Distinguish the reason. Missing, malformed, or stale registration needs a
   scoped configuration repair. An aligned registration with no tools in the
   active session needs a restart/reconnection; doctor cannot prove that the
   current agent has connected. A missing provider affects only tasks requiring
   that provider: static JavaScript inspection needs neither Hopper nor Ghidra,
   and Android inspection has separate bring-your-own JADX/Java prerequisites.
3. For a configuration repair, prepare the read-only plan:
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0 setup --client codex --dry-run --json`.
   Use the current client's ID, show its exact proposed paths, backups, and
   changes, and obtain approval before setup writes configuration or installs
   Hopper. Setup normally installs the matching bundled skill too; include that
   replacement in the reviewed plan. After approval, apply the same scope with
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0 setup --client codex --yes`. Add `--install-hopper`
   only if that separate installation was needed and explicitly approved.
4. Restart/reconnect the affected agent. Verify that REA tools actually appear
   in the session, then resume the original investigation. If they remain
   absent, inspect the client's MCP launch error rather than repeating setup.

REA setup never installs or upgrades Node.js, npm, Homebrew, Java, Ghidra, IDA,
JADX, Binwalk, or Unblob. Use existing prerequisites; do not install unrelated
software to repair
MCP registration. For an unsupported client, use manual stdio registration
with a version-pinned `rea-agents` package or continue through the CLI.

A concrete CLI fallback for an operator-supplied JavaScript tree or ASAR is:

```bash
npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0 analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json
```

No MCP registration or native engine is required. Read the returned Evidence,
graph, limitations, and unknowns with the same care as an MCP result; the CLI
returns the Evidence record directly. This fallback does not establish that
MCP is configured. Native CLI tasks still require their selected engine.
Prefer an existing `rea` CLI. When none is installed and REA package acquisition
is within the authorized scope, use `npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0` in its place.
Configuration repair starts with a read-only setup plan; show paths, backups and
skill replacement before applying authorized changes. Preserve existing approval
and target-execution boundaries. REA setup never installs or upgrades unrelated
software, including Node.js, npm, Homebrew, Java, Ghidra, IDA, JADX, Binwalk or Unblob.

## Route the target first

Choose the first tool from the target the user supplied. Use `open_binary` for
active-target native or archive workflows; target-free tools take their own
explicit path or endpoint and do not need it.

- ASAR or extracted JavaScript/Electron tree:
  `analyze_javascript_application`.
- Archive/package member inventory (ZIP/APK/IPA/MSIX/AppX or DMG):
  `open_binary` with the supplied local path; use `inspect_artifact` when its
  graph and findings help answer the question.
- Android APK code, classes, methods, or incoming references:
  `inspect_android_package`, then focused Android tools when advertised.
  Archive member inventory still uses the archive route above.
- Managed PE/CLI assembly: `inspect_managed_artifact`.
- Firmware image: `inspect_firmware_regions` when advertised. Use
  `extract_firmware` when extraction is requested, with a caller-selected new
  absolute output directory. These tools use caller-supplied Binwalk/Unblob on
  Linux; see the [firmware guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/firmware-analysis.md).
- .NET NativeAOT PE/ELF: native Ghidra analysis. Native code can yield pseudocode;
  consult the NativeAOT workflow in `references/native-and-artifacts.md` for
  optional metadata recovery and its supported host/layout boundary.
- User-owned browser page already open: `list_browser_targets`.
- Browser action the agent must perform (click, type, navigate):
  `capture_browser_scenario` with declared actions. See
  [runtime observation](references/runtime-observation.md) for connect/launch
  and the focused follow-up browser tools.
- Fiddler Everywhere traffic or a native `.saz` capture: read the
  [Fiddler workflow](references/runtime-observation.md#fiddler-everywhere-traffic-debugging).
  Inspect saved SAZ with `inspect_web_network_capture` and `format: "saz"`;
  connect Everywhere's separate MCP server for live traffic.
- Retained HAR/SAZ/native mitmproxy/aioquic qlog capture: `inspect_web_network_capture`. Select
  original record ordinals when useful; inspect producer fields and byte/number
  sidecars without fetching recorded URLs or claiming live attribution. See
  [historical captures](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/web-network-captures.md) for the exact upstream
  profile and credential exclusions. Qlog support starts with aioquic 1.5.0
  JSON 0.3; stream coverage and endpoint loss declarations do not recover bodies
  or establish network loss. Prefer detail summary, then kind qlog trace/stream
  pages; select one trace, stream ID and direction for contribution/range pages.
  Facts retain all-recorded-events-before-selection scope. Other qlog layouts
  and PCAP correlation are unsupported.
- User-owned Electron runtime already open: `list_electron_targets`. Before an electron-main Inspector attempt, check packaged fuses with `inspect_electron_fuses`; disabled `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments` means the app ignores `--inspect`.
- Packet-field discovery: `inspect_packet_fields` searches installed protocols
  and field names/types before choosing fields for `inspect_packet_capture`.
  Query/page the relevant records; registrations do not establish observed traffic.
- Recorded packet captures: `inspect_packet_capture` with selected TShark fields,
  display filters and decode-as rules. Requires Linux, util-linux prlimit and `REA_TSHARK_COMMAND`; see
  [capture guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/packet-captures.md).
  Packet limits count input packets before filtering. Output defaults to 50 matching
  frames; use `match_offset` / `match_limit` for later pages, or explicit null
  limit for complete matching output. Preserve the source digest across pages.
  This does not perform live capture.
  For address/DNS/SNI/protocol summaries use `inspect_pcap_capture` with MCP
  detail summary, then retained kind pcap pages. Requires Wireshark 4.x tshark
  and capinfos, with Linux prlimit or Windows Job Objects; see
  [packet summaries](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/pcap-analysis.md).
  Select an exact DNS question for address pages; page exhaustion does not prove
  network completeness. This reads recordings and does not acquire traffic.
- Decoder discovery: `inspect_signal_decoders` searches installed decoder IDs
  or selected decoder help, including channels and options. Query and page the
  relevant details before choosing settings; this does not scan hardware.
- Recorded logic/signal traces: `decode_signal_recording` with explicit decoder,
  channel and protocol settings. On Linux with util-linux prlimit, supply sigrok-cli 0.7.2 through
  `REA_SIGROK_COMMAND`; see [recording guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/signal-recordings.md).
  Output defaults to 50 literal lines; select annotation classes and page with
  `line_offset` / `line_limit`, or explicit null for all remaining output.
  Window counts are display lines, not annotations or samples. Preserve source digests across pages.
  This reads existing files; it does not acquire hardware signals.
- Explicit local WebAssembly artifact: `inspect_wasm_artifact`. Supply WABT 1.0.42
  through `REA_WABT_BIN_DIRECTORY`; retain exact byte/tool identity and decoded WAT.
  Select JavaScript glue and candidate paths explicitly and preserve URL/path
  ambiguity. No implicit fetch or target execution; WAT is not original source.
  See the [WASM guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/wasm-artifacts.md).
- Explicit local EVM bytecode carrier: `inspect_evm_interface` with caller-selected
  `raw` or `hex` encoding. Preserve carrier/decoded digests and treat selectors,
  argument strings and mutability as inferred candidates; this performs no chain
  lookup or target execution. For the complete inferred interface without hex or
  duplicate stdout, discover support and select `detail: "summary"`; complete
  Evidence stays retained under its original identity. Use the returned
  `parent_evidence_id` for exact function or `bytecode_hex`/stdout/stderr pages.
  Candidate coverage does not establish interface completeness. See the
  [EVM bytecode guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/evm-bytecode.md).
- Embedded Go compiler, module or build-setting metadata: `inspect_go_binary`
  with the explicit local file. This built-in target-free inspection requires no
  Go installation or disassembler. Preserve raw module bytes and source ranges;
  absent metadata does not prove a binary is not Go, and unparsed text records
  remain explicit. See the
  [Go binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/go-binaries.md).
- Embedded cargo-auditable Rust dependency metadata: `inspect_rust_binary`
  with the explicit local ELF, PE, or thin Mach-O file. This built-in
  target-free inspection requires no Rust installation or disassembler. Preserve
  package order, dependency indices, and the section file range. A missing
  `.dep-v0` section is null metadata, not proof the binary has no dependencies.
  A rustc commit hash is an inference from a read-only `/rustc/<40-hex>/` path.
  See the
  [Rust binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/rust-binaries.md).

- Explicit local SQLite database snapshot: `inspect_sqlite_database`. Inspect
  with Node.js 24.x >=24.15 or 26+ providing native SQLite limits. Read schema
  first (compact inventory by default), or select an exact ordinary table
  and `columns` when rows are needed. Defaults are selected-table schema and
  20 rows; request `schema_scope: "database"` for the complete stored schema. Preserve both database and existing sibling WAL identity; row samples
  report truncation and have unspecified order. Use a quiescent snapshot rather
  than assuming a live database/WAL pair was copied atomically. See the
  [SQLite guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/sqlite-databases.md).
- Explicit Linux ELF file for offline layout, symbols, relocations or static
  mitigation evidence: `inspect_binary_layout`. This target-free operation uses
  caller-supplied pwntools without opening a disassembler database. Preserve its
  raw locations and inference/coverage limits; see the
  [offline binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/binary-diagnostics.md).
- Supplied Linux x86-64 ELF core: `inspect_recorded_crash`. Read every recorded
  thread, raw note and source-bound register without opening a live target.
  Historical PIDs do not select live processes. Request `include_debugger_context`
  only when core-only mapping candidates help; see the
  [recorded crash guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/recorded-crashes.md).
- PE resource type/name/language trees and static icon group references:
  `inspect_pe_resources` with an explicit path. This portable operation requires
  no active target or engine; opaque payloads retain file ranges and SHA-256.
- Native executable, library, or analysis database: `open_binary`, then
  use focused analysis tools directly; call `binary_overview` when metadata or
  inventory context is useful and available from the selected provider.

For an existing IDA MCP configuration, use `open_binary` with the original
input binary and `provider_id: "ida"`; do not pass an `.idb` or `.i64` database.
The legacy attached profile binds the already-open GUI input by SHA-256 and
leaves its database open. The modern headless profile creates and closes an
owned private database without saving. Installation and registration reuse
[mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp](https://github.com/mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp); see the
[IDA provider guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/ida-provider.md).
Proceed directly to `analyze_function`, pseudocode, or function/string searches
after opening; IDA does not supply `binary_overview`. Consult session availability
when composing broader workflows. Modern direct callers and unsupported dossier
facets remain unknown; live IDA results are not replayed from snapshots.

If the user says only "my app" without a name, path, or target already selected
for this task, ask which app before searching for artifacts. Paths in unrelated
saved reports and nearby test fixtures do not select the user's target. Resolve
an actual human-readable app name to one clear installed artifact when possible;
ask when matches are ambiguous. Never choose an example app on the user's behalf.

In a target-free session, use `open_binary` to bind any archive/package or
native target whose analysis tool operates on the active target. Do not call an
unadvertised tool; inspect `binary_session` with `{}` and its
`result.tool_availability` for availability reasons and remediation. Expand each
group's `names` into entries, inheriting the inventory-level client requirements
unless the group overrides them. In its closed effect and annotation vocabularies,
listed flags are true and omitted known flags are false. The grouped name union
is the complete tool inventory; use `tools/list` for canonical tool schemas.
Provider candidate facts describe possible providers, while top-level session
capabilities describe the current route and `analysis_provider_binding` names the
selected provider. Do not treat those scopes as interchangeable.

## Work summary-first

Start with the default result and use its inline Evidence and graph context.
For a JavaScript application or ELF layout whose size is unknown or large,
call `analyze_javascript_application` or `inspect_binary_layout` with
`"detail": "summary"`, then inspect the retained `parent_evidence_id` with
`inspect_analysis_view`.
Page module identities and select the returned `node_id` before requesting an
item; a single file path can represent several graph roles. Do not repeat an
identical analysis or rejected call without a changed input or resolved blocker.
Recheck session state when a lifecycle change makes that status useful.
Make a focused follow-up only when the
returned result leaves a specific question unanswered.

If MCP reports `resource_constraint` with `details.resource: "transport"`, call
`inspect_analysis_view` with its reported same-session Evidence reference for a
summary, one section/module, or a stable page. Use `trace_application_feature`
once a seed is known, or call `export_evidence_bundle` to write the complete
session to a selected path. The analysis remains complete in the ledger; avoid
repeating it merely to request the same oversized response. Complete CLI JSON
output also streams without a single MCP frame.

When the retained parent ID is unknown, use `get_evidence_bundle` with
`detail: "summary"` and exact filters for operation, target SHA-256,
analysis-profile digest or canonical procedure address. Select its returned
Evidence ID for the next view instead of requesting the complete bundle.
`retention: "complete-record"` means the whole record is stored; native
value-flow truncation and unknown metadata remain separate. For an exported
portable bundle, use `rea inspect-evidence-bundle` with JSON containing `path`,
`detail: "summary"` and the same `filters`. Reading that file still requires
validating its full contents within the local memory budget.

A client can also truncate a successful tool result without a REA transport
error. Treat that preview as incomplete; use the retained parent ID for smaller
views or export when the full record is needed. Do not parse the preview as
canonical JSON or repeat the producer. For JavaScript, read the
[module-view and trace recipes](references/javascript-applications.md) before
drilling into a large graph; a broad bidirectional trace can expand unrelated
containment relationships even after summary analysis.

Every conclusion must distinguish observations, inferences, and unknowns. Cite
Evidence IDs, preserve limitations and incomplete coverage, and never imply
that static analysis observed execution. Runtime requests execute the declared
target and lifecycle; do not broaden the target or action beyond those fields.

Within the user's requested investigation, call available analysis tools
directly. REA does not require permission grants or per-call approval flags.
The agent client can independently require approval. Follow the declared request
scope and the host's actual access requirements; use the recovery guide for an
observed client-policy rejection.

## Plan broader investigations

For requests that span multiple features or subsystems, use a staged workflow:

1. Turn the request into a checklist of questions and the evidence each answer
   needs. Resolve target identity and constraints from the conversation and
   workspace before asking for information again.
2. Inspect the current REA session, artifact identity, saved analysis database,
   bookmarks, and prior evidence. Reuse matching state; do not open duplicate
   sessions or repeat identical analysis.
3. Start with the smallest useful overview or inventory. Follow each question
   from its entry point through relevant data and state changes to its result.
   Batch related operations around a specific hypothesis, then expand only when
   the returned evidence leaves a concrete gap.
4. Inspect relevant packaged resources and configuration alongside code when
   they affect the question. Use format-aware inventory and parsers; do not
   infer behavior from filenames, strings, or layout alone.
5. Corroborate a conclusion with the evidence type it requires. Use runtime
   observation only when static evidence cannot answer the question and the
   required host runtime and OS access are available. For JavaScript behavior,
   run probes against the actual app through the available browser, Electron,
   or process capture workflow.
6. Decompose work into independent questions. When parallel workers are
   available and the questions do not depend on one another, assign distinct
   scopes, point workers to existing evidence, and ask them to return sources,
   conclusions, and unresolved gaps. Otherwise, work sequentially.
7. Keep a concise finding ledger linking each conclusion to Evidence IDs,
   confidence/evidence type, search boundary, and remaining unknowns. Update
   the shared index or investigation report so later passes can reuse results.

Before finishing, revisit the original checklist. Mark each question as
answered, partially answered, or unresolved based on its evidence; keep
bounded negative searches bounded, and do not describe a broad investigation
as complete while required questions remain open.

## Read only the relevant guide

- Native binaries, managed assemblies, archives, and extraction:
  [references/native-and-artifacts.md](references/native-and-artifacts.md)
- ASARs, extracted JavaScript, feature tracing, and version comparison:
  [references/javascript-applications.md](references/javascript-applications.md)
- Android APK declarations, classes, methods, and static references:
  [references/android-applications.md](references/android-applications.md)
- Browser/Electron observation (passive and scenario) and static/runtime
  reconciliation:
  [references/runtime-observation.md](references/runtime-observation.md)
- Evidence paging, comparisons, residual unknowns, and verification:
  [references/evidence-workflows.md](references/evidence-workflows.md)

## Finish the task

Explain findings in plain language and tie them to returned evidence. When the
user asks to build something, use normal coding tools and separate observed
behavior from design choices. Close an opened native session with
`close_binary` when the investigation is complete.

commands.name: session-chat
commands.description: Treat the other conversations open in MCode as contacts - consult one that holds context this work needs, hand a piece of work to one, keep a long-running conversation's purpose and task up to date, or open a new conversation for a separate strand of work. Use when the user asks to ask, tell, consult or coordinate with another conversation, or when what you need is known to a conversation that is not this one.
commands.template:
# Talking to other conversations

Every conversation open in MCode is a contact with its own history, its own
folder and its own turn. Messaging one runs a real turn there, which the user
can watch; the reply is that turn's final message.

This is not delegation. A helper that does one piece of work and disappears is
the `task` tool's job - a subagent shares this conversation's turn and cannot
use these tools at all. Reach for a session only when the work belongs to a
conversation that outlives this turn: one that already holds the context, or one
the user keeps for that strand of work.

## Finding who to talk to

`contacts` lists the others, most recently active first. Each line gives the
title, the contact id, whether it is busy, and the purpose, workspace, task and
task status recorded for it.

Call it when you cannot name the target exactly, when you want to read what a
conversation is for, or after `talk_to_session` came back with candidates. When
you already know the exact title or the id, skip it and send the message.

## Sending a message

`talk_to_session` takes either `contact` (the target's exact title) or
`contact_id`, and a `message`.

- The other conversation cannot see this one. Write the message so it stands on
  its own: what you need, what it is for, and any detail from here it would
  otherwise have to ask for.
- `mode: "sync"` is the default and waits up to 120 seconds. If the target is
  busy, or the reply does not come in time, the call returns at once and says it
